bibliography.abstract: Faculty hiring shapes the research, teaching, and advising capacity of transportation engineering, but field-specific evidence on academic hiring pathways remains limited. This paper provides a descriptive case study of how doctoral training institutions map to first tenure-track faculty appointments in U.S. transportation-focused civil engineering. Using publicly available records, we construct a reproducible cross-sectional dataset linking faculty members to their doctoral institutions and first tenure-track academic appointments. We measure institutional prestige using a five-tier scheme based on U.S. News civil engineering rankings and summarize doctoral tier to first-hire tier transitions, upward and downward mobility, and variation in placement concentration across doctoral programs. We also estimate ordered logit models to summarize the association between doctoral tier and first-hire tier while controlling for doctoral completion cohort and broad educational background characteristics available from public records. Results show substantial persistence in initial placement, with many hires occurring within the same or an adjacent tier. At the same time, the system is not closed: upward mobility occurs from lower-ranked doctoral tiers, and many first hires occur at institutions outside the ranked set. Model estimates show a monotone prestige gradient that is stable to cohort and background controls and that persists across doctoral completion cohorts. The findings provide a benchmark for understanding doctoral-to-faculty hiring pathways in transportation civil engineering. Rather than estimating causal effects, the study documents how first-hire outcomes are associated with doctoral prestige and identifies areas where greater placement transparency, mentoring, and professional visibility could support transportation workforce development.
bibliography.title: Who hires whom? A case study of prestige stratification in U.S. transportation faculty hiring

en.caveats: The study is descriptive and correlational rather than causal, and it relies on a five-tier prestige proxy derived from a single ranking system.
en.what: This study analyzes the relationship between doctoral training institutions and first tenure-track faculty appointments for U.S. transportation civil engineering faculty. Using a reproducible cross-sectional dataset built from public records, the researchers categorized institutional prestige into five tiers based on U.S. News civil engineering rankings and modeled placement outcomes using ordered logit regression. The analysis reveals a strong, stable prestige gradient where many hires occur within the same or adjacent tiers, though upward mobility from lower-ranked tiers and placements outside the ranked set also occur.
en.why: It establishes a baseline empirical benchmark for academic hiring pathways specifically within transportation engineering, showing that institutional prestige remains a persistent factor in faculty placement across different cohorts.
